abstract: This study examines how the rise of large language models and generative AI affects labor market outcomes for recent college graduates by comparing employment, earnings, and job switching patterns across college majors with different levels of AI exposure before and after ChatGPT's introduction in November 2022. Using administrative records on 6.7 million bachelor's degree graduates from 350+ institutions covering 29% of U.S. degrees conferred from 2016-2024, the authors find that graduates in the most AI-exposed majors experienced immediate and significant declines in initial employment rates and earnings following ChatGPT's release. The most AI-exposed decile saw a five percentage point decline in employment probability and thirteen percent decline in full-quarter earnings, comparable to graduating into a large recession, with roughly half of earnings losses attributable to sectoral shifts toward lower-wage industries.
keyFindings: Graduates in the top decile of AI-exposed majors experienced a five percentage point decline in initial employment and thirteen percent decline in quarterly earnings following ChatGPT's introduction in November 2022, compared to less-exposed majors.

Employment effects concentrated in the tenth decile (primarily computer science, information systems, and software development majors) with effects attenuating more gradually than deciles seven through nine.

Approximately half of the earnings decline for the most exposed graduates resulted from shifts into lower-paying industry sectors (Retail Trade, Accommodation & Food Services) away from high-paying sectors (Information, Professional Services), indicating underemployment rather than wage cuts alone.

Effects begin to attenuate by four quarters post-graduation (one year) but remain substantial at eight quarters (two years) post-graduation for the most exposed decile, suggesting temporary but persistent short-term labor market disruption.
The magnitude of short-term earnings and employment losses for AI-exposed graduates is comparable to the effects of entering the labor market during a large recession.
methodology: Administrative data study using U.S. Census Bureau sources: (1) Post-Secondary Employment Outcomes (PSEO) data covering 6,665,500 bachelor's degree graduates from 27 data partners across 24 states and 350+ institutions from 2016-2024; (2) American Community Survey (ACS) 2018-2022 data restricted to workers aged 21-29 with bachelor's degrees to construct occupation-weighted major-level AI exposure measures; (3) Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics (LEHD) data from state Unemployment Insurance wage records and QCEW covering 48 states through Q3 2025. AI exposure measured using Eloundou et al. (2024) GPT-4 Beta task-level exposure scores aggregated to occupations and then occupation-weighted to college majors using ACS occupation distributions. Event-study design with high-dimensional fixed effects model including institution-major interactions, institution-quarter effects, and major-quarter-of-year effects, comparing outcomes across exposure deciles relative to 2022 baseline before and after November 2022 ChatGPT release. Sample size: 6,665,500 graduates with linked employment histories through 2025.
qualifiers: Authors note that results represent a subset of institutions—primarily public, research-intensive doctoral-granting universities—which are overrepresented relative to the U.S. postsecondary landscape (29% of bachelor's degrees), limiting generalizability to other institution types if AI effects are heterogeneous. Limited time window since ChatGPT release (approximately 2 years maximum follow-up for 2024 data) restricts ability to assess long-term career trajectories or whether exposed graduates eventually catch up to peers. AI exposure measures predate newer model innovations and agentic platforms, serving as snapshots of rapidly evolving technology. Study excludes Alaska and Michigan due to incomplete LEHD data coverage. Results do not distinguish between changes in AI capability intensity versus changing labor market responses over time. Parallel trends assumption requires absence of confounding shocks affecting top deciles around ChatGPT release; alternative explanations (remote work, monetary policy, industry shocks) addressed but not completely ruled out. General equilibrium effects potentially violate SUTVA, and results are reduced-form estimates. Alaska and Michigan residents excluded from employment rate calculations, which should be interpreted as likelihood of UI-covered employment outside these states.
